newsitem.title: KENYA: Man killed as Kenya strike finds little success.
newsitem.headline: Man killed as Kenya strike finds little success.

text.p: Pro-opposition youths beat a man to death at a Nairobi rally and looted elsewhere in Kenya on Friday but a national strike to press for constitutional reforms had little success.
Barely 1,000 activists attended a rally in Nairobi's Uhuru park to hear opposition speakers demand sweeping political reforms from President Daniel arap Moi before elections due this year.
At the rally, gangs of youths ran down and beat up several people suspected of being police spies, including Gilbert Ahanya Simiyi. He was pronounced dead on arrival at Nairobi Hospital.
Opposition supporters said Simiyi was an inspector in the police special branch. Police declined to comment on the report.

At the rally's end, hundreds of youths took to the city centre, breaking shop windows and chanting "Moi must go". They stoned vehicles and set up barricades until paramilitary General Service Unit police fired in the air and dispersed them.

Most city centre shops were closed and some workers stayed at home. But shop owners, many from the Asian community, said they closed for fear of the violence and looting which is customary at political mass protests in Kenya.
Overall the national strike and protest marches called by opposition-backed groups pushing for political reforms had scant success.
Moi's government declared the strike and demonstrations unlawful but police did not intervene to stop the Nairobi rally.
In the city's vast Mathare slum unemployed youths set barricades of burning tyres and clashed with riot police. They also attacked a bar as it stayed open and looted iron sheets.
They tried to join the rally in the park but were barred from marching through the Eastleigh suburb by ethnic Somalis.
Witnesses reported clashes and some looting in the towns of Nyahururu, Karatina, Kerugoya, Thika, Nyeri, Kiambu and Githunguri in the opposition heartland of Central Province.

Crowds of demonstrators marched in the western town of Kisumu and the Rift Valley town of Nakuru but calm returned when police intervened. Two opposition FORD-Kenya parliamentarians were arrested in Kisumu allegedly for inciting people to strike.
The port of Mombasa, the East African country's second city, was calm with only a few shops closed, residents said.
Tension has risen steadily in the past two months and at least nine people were killed on July 7 when security forces suppressed pro-reform protests in Nairobi and other centres.
The shilling sank to an historic official low against the dollar on Thursday but regained 1.76 percent by Friday's close, standing at a commercial mean of 69.02 to the dollar.

But traders said the currency was still fragile and it was too soon to talk of a recovery. The shilling has lost nearly 16 percent since the International Monetary Fund shelved a $205 million loan last week because of official corruption.

Moi, 73 and in power since 1978, is seeking a final five-year term at elections this year. Under pressure at home and from Western donors, he agreed to some reforms before the polls, succeeding in dividing some opposition party leaders.
In a speech in central Kenya, Moi said on Friday his government was committed to eradicating corruption in Kenya and added that all those involved would be fully investigated.
